SmartUp Foundations Course - Lecture 13
Given January 2nd, 2025, by Yonatan Stern

A few announcements. First of all, it's a bit shocking for me to see we are on lecture number 13, and surprisingly, I still have a lot more to talk about — so you'll have to bear with me. Second, we asked you for feedback. We got some feedback, which was very interesting and important for us, but we didn't get feedback from each and every one of you. So those of you who want to be here next time, please send your feedback, or else we're going to chase you.

So this lecture is about my favorite subject, which is you — or you as a representative of people. As you will see in the next two hours, people are really complicated, and that's why they kill most businesses. It's the people that kill the businesses. So I have here employees and customers.

This lecture will only deal with the employees, which is one big problem. The customers I'll hopefully get to next time or the time after. And I will explain why customers are also people and therefore are also a problem. But I'll start with the usual. That's our team. Ayala is hiding over there, and I strongly recommend you get to know her because she manages my life. So if you need anything from me, Ayala is the right person. And obviously, Libby. What we do here is — as you can see — I added the word "engineering" to the profession, not just the profession. Why the word "engineering"? Because I'm trying to build a methodology that is like engineering. You can measure everything, you can plan everything. It's not just statements. As I've said many, many times, a successful company is a company that first and foremost is profitable.

It is fast-growing — not like a family business that doesn't go anywhere — and it needs a modest investment. And what we do here is work with companies. Right now we have — I don't remember exactly — four, five, or six companies that we work with in a residency program. And it's growing nicely.

So I'll start with the agenda. The title, I think, tells you everything. It's the most complex part of your job, and the reason is that people are unique. We'll get to that in a moment. Then I will share a lot of personal stories from my experience working with people, mainly because everything that has to do with people is personal.

I'll go into the personal side of it, talk about leadership — what leadership does to a company and how do you run a company. My second favorite subject is co-founders. For those of you who don't know my opinion, you will hear it about 10 times during this presentation — how important co-founders are — and team size: how many people do you want to hire, when do you want to hire them, why do you want to hire them, and so on. And if we talk about hiring — what are your criteria when you hire? All the dilemmas that every company faces as they start hiring, the process of firing, compensation issues, how do you pay, what do you pay for, morale issues.

And obviously you're not a manager unless you fire some people, because before that you are just playing at being a manager. But when you need to sit down and tell somebody, "I'm sorry, but as of tomorrow, you're not here," then you start to understand the difficulties. So we have a heavy agenda — let's get started.

I'm sure you have all heard this: "Business would be so easy if not for the employees and the customers," right? If you haven't heard that statement, you haven't been around long enough. And the most important asset that you have is your team. At the beginning, many entrepreneurs start on their own, so their team is just one person. But most of us have a hard time doing everything ourselves.

So we start surrounding ourselves with a team — whether it's co-founders or, later on, people we hire. And that really becomes your most important asset. Building an effective team is very difficult. And I will go into that later. Why is it so complicated to build a successful team? Beyond that, remember — to be a successful company, you have to be profitable. Profitable means you have a revenue line and an expense line, and revenue minus expenses is your profit. And what are your expenses? In most cases, 70 to 80% of your expenses are salaries and everything around them. And they represent 100% of your success or failure.

So really it's all about the people — the salaries you pay and what you get out of them — which is why people are so critical to the business. So if you want to start measuring things, I've put this slide up before. "Mathematics is the language in which God has written the universe." That's Galileo Galilei, for those who don't recognize the picture. He was the first person who actually wrote an equation in physics. Until then, people talked about it in philosophical terms — things tend to do X, tend to do Y, tend to fall, tend to jump. He was the first one who started measuring and finding the correlation between two things. Later on, Newton built on that and wrote the famous equation f=ma. Those of you who don't know what that means, please come to me after the session and I will explain what f=ma means.

So that changed the world. And the language of business, obviously, is money. And money is something you can measure. Those of you who don't know how to measure money, talk to your spouse, because you have a big problem — and I can't solve that problem. But money you can calculate. You can calculate your income, you can calculate your expenses. And it's critical to convert everything you do to money, because that's really the equation that tells you: are you going in the right direction? Are you going the wrong direction? What the hell are you doing? So when you hire a person, you have to look at the cost and all the other expenses around it.

So again — people are complicated. The question is why. And the answer is something we all know, but I don't think we really understand the consequences. We all understand that each and every one of us is unique — we are each the whole world, right? As far as I'm concerned, I'm the only person in the world, and the rest of you are just bothering me. And each and every one of you feels the same — to you, I'm just a nuisance, bothering you. And that's the reality. We are all unique. Now you want to put all of these unique people in one room and try to aim them in one direction. And it's complicated — it's just very complicated. And anybody who ignores that complexity is making a big mistake.

So if we start with this assumption — and you will start seeing the consequences in a moment — the first consequence is a little bit of modesty. And I'm getting personal here, because I don't want to tell you that you don't know what you're doing, but I can tell you I don't know what I'm doing. That's fair enough. I'm not aware of any reliable way to predict people's performance in your company. You hire, you pray, you hope, and you are surprised — always. For better or for worse. You can be surprised for the better. I'm not saying you're always surprised for the worse, but what you get is never what you expected. At least in my case, never. Sometimes it's better, sometimes it's worse. Unfortunately, most times it's worse, because you try to hire the best person possible for the job and you find surprises.

Those of you who work in bigger companies, they have this annual review, right? So stop laughing. It's the end of the year, you start having — you know — this annual review, and you get a form with 10 pages, 360-degree feedback, and whatever else it is. And the reality is, in my companies, there was never an annual review. Why? Because I just don't believe it represents anything real. They go through the motions, but it's never real. So I just don't do it. It's very hard to quantify a person. It's just impossible.

So from here on, for about the next 20 minutes, I'm going to talk about my own perspective. Because every person is unique, I can only speak from my own perspective. Each and every one of you, as I talk, think about similar experiences that you've had.

ZoomInfo. ZoomInfo was founded in 2000. At that time, we were living in Boston — me, my wife, and my three daughters. And we decided it was about time to move back to Israel. My kids say we didn't move back — we made Aliyah. I moved back. And my daughter, who is right here, was approaching eighth grade. The following year she was going to go to high school. And we said, that's it — we have to go back to Israel or we'll never go back. The company was four years old at that point. I was very worried. That was before Zoom, before all of these technologies. I was very worried about how I was going to run the company from Israel while everybody was in Boston. I was the only person in Israel. So I decided to bring in a president in the US to run the operation — the whole operation was in Boston — and I would fly back and forth. That was the idea.

I brought in a person — Gary, as you can see — in 2003. I brought him in a year before I left, so I'd have time to work with him and make sure we were on the same wavelength. And I brought in a really highly accomplished guy. He was the CEO at Thomson Business Intelligence for four years — from 1997 to 2001. So I brought him to ZoomInfo and we started working together.

About a year into our relationship — with me in Israel and him in Boston — I started to realize that we didn't have the same definitions about profitability, about what needed to be done. I basically lost confidence in the guy. He lost confidence in me, and we decided that the best solution was to part ways. So we parted ways. And you would assume, yeah, he was a bad guy, a stupid idiot. So here's what the "stupid idiot" did — he went and started a competitive company called Net Prospects. But he had a better idea than me on how to build the company. We had built it based on technology — reading the internet, extracting information — don't ask, it was almost like sending a man to the moon. He did something a lot simpler.

He went to companies that had very big databases of subscribers, like magazines. And he said: "If you give me your list, I'll give you the same number of leads that you don't have. We'll just swap." So he started building very rapidly a really good list of people — phone numbers, addresses, email addresses — just by swapping and having rights to all those names. And to add insult to injury, he also verified that the data was correct. So when he was trading, he would take the file that he got, send it to India. They picked 500 names at random, picked up the phone, sent an email, and his criterion was 90% accuracy. If your list was not 90% accurate and current, he wouldn't take it. His company was doing really well.
Having a right to all of these names. And to add another insult to me, he also verified that the data is correct. So when he was trading, he would take the file that he got, send it to India. They picked 500 names at random, picked up the phone, sent an email, and his criteria was 90% accuracy. If your list was not 90% accurate and current, he wouldn't take it. His company was doing really well.

While I was still working hard at ZoomInfo, he sold the company to Dun & Bradstreet for $120 million. He had an exit way before me at a really nice price. And as you can see, I was very right at hiring him. It didn't work out. So that's president number one.

Now let's look at president number two, Brian. He was president from 2006 to 2008, and I brought him from Monster. Monster was a very large company — actually the largest company at the time dealing with recruiting. They had a very large database of resumes. Everybody who wanted a job put their resume in Monster, because every HR department in every company was a subscriber of Monster. That's the way people got a job, or were hired. So he was the Chief Marketing Officer, and he definitely knew the market we were going after.

I brought him to ZoomInfo to be president in 2006. And true to nature, because he came from a big company like Monster, he started building divisions at ZoomInfo. I had three different groups with group managers that he hired because he knew them. Before I knew it, there was a big company structure over there — except it just didn't perform well. In 2008, I said to the guy, "Listen, Brian, I'm sorry, but this is not the way to go. I have to ask you to move aside." So I didn't fire him. He became the Chief of Corporate Development, because he was a phenomenal salesman, and he was with the company from 2008 to 2010. But along the way, we spun off another company called Bizo, and the VP of Marketing at ZoomInfo became the CEO of Bizo. And he wanted to take Brian with him.

So I said, "Hey, go ahead." So he joined Bizo, and Bizo was very successful. In 2014, it was sold to LinkedIn. So as you can see, very successful guy. Now he's the CEO of a company called ClearGuard. So again, Jonathan just took a really good guy, ruined him. When I let him go, he was brilliant and good again. So that's president number two.

But the saga continues. President number three, Sam. Because I had already two failures, right? Two. So the board said, "Sorry, Jonathan, but you're really bad at hiring, so let us help you." So this guy Sam had built a company for me called BuyerZone. The chairman of that company was on my board. He said, "This guy did a phenomenal job. He took that company — it was going nowhere — and he built it, and we sold it for $43 million to another company. He's phenomenal. You won't make a mistake here." So I sat down with Sam. I liked him, nice guy, and hired him.

So he was with me for three years, and you can kind of guess where I'm going, right? The company was not doing well. I had a meeting with Sam and I said, "Sam, I'm sorry, this is not working." And he said, "Yeah, you're right." And he was so disillusioned with ZoomInfo that he wanted to return all of his shares. He didn't want to have anything to do with ZoomInfo anymore — period, done. And he left. Then he joined a company called CarGurus. He's the COO, and he's doing phenomenally well. He's done very well over there and is very successful.

So what can you see here? The people I brought in were the right people, really smart. I just — I don't know — my problem, probably. And then after I let them go, they started to flourish again. Why am I saying all of that? Because it's a matter of just working together. These are really smart people. I'm still friends with some of them, and it just didn't work out. Not my fault, not their fault — sort of.

So when I told the board that I let Sam go, one of my board members said, "You know, Jonathan, these are three wonderful people. The only constant in this story is you. So maybe we are firing the wrong people." And I said, "Potentially." But because I knew this was coming — when I built the company, there was a clause that certain things needed to have my shares voting for it, and one of them was firing the CEO. So I left the room, walked out, came back, and I said, "I checked with the holders of Class A shares, and they don't vote for letting the CEO go." And he said, "Why am I not surprised?"

So we didn't have many more board meetings afterwards. It was kind of the end of the board meetings, and at the end, everything turned out to be good. They still talk to me. But beside that story, I think this is very illuminating on these issues — and I have more stories like that.

So before ZoomInfo, I had another company called CardScan. It was founded in '93 and was acquired in 2006. Notice the overlap in times — I ran the two of them in parallel. The company started out selling mainly direct. We put a lot of ads, people would call on the phone, and we would sell them the product. But obviously, if you want to grow with a product that's just a small scanner costing $250, you need to get into stores. I had no clue whatsoever how to sell through Office Depot and Staples and CompUSA and all of that. I just didn't know what to do. So I hired a guy who knew. His name is Steve. He was VP of Sales from 1995 to 1997, brought the company to about $6 million in sales, and then kind of plateaued. He'd reached the maximum I thought he could take us to.

So — same story again. I had a conversation with him and said, "Steve, I'm sorry, but we have to part ways." So he left. It was the heyday of the dot-com boom, so he started a company called Anyday.com. Anyday.com was basically — how do you call it — a calendar on the web. So he called me and said, "Jonathan, I need some advice." I said, "Okay, what's the scoop?" He said, "How do I make money here?" I said, "Honestly, I don't understand why anybody needs a diary on the web, but I don't know." So we sat down and tried to brainstorm, and I had no idea how you make money on a calendar on the web.

But it was the heyday — everybody was running around. He had Anyday.com and he started talking with Palm Pilot. Now, you know what a Palm Pilot is — it's a small handheld computer. They really wanted to acquire Anyday.com because they wanted to have a calendar on the web and sync it with the Palm Pilot. They agreed on a price of $80 million. Palm Pilot wanted to pay in cash, and Anyday.com wanted it in Palm Pilot shares because the shares were worth more. But Palm Pilot said, "We don't give shares, we give cash." So there was an argument, and at the end of the day Palm Pilot won, and they paid in cash, and the company was acquired.

Steve left the company with $20-something million dollars in his pocket, fairly happy, and that was it. Then one day I was talking to the board and told them this story, and one of my board members said, "I know this story — I was the one negotiating that deal." I said, "What?" He said, "Yeah, I was the one negotiating the deal." And so I got all the details I had missed from him.

So here's another great example that I'm very good at hiring people and very bad at doing the right things with them. He's a really nice guy, Steve. Lesson learned: people are different in different situations, and their performance can vary radically. And the reason I brought all of these stories is to tell you — I'm not just saying it, I really lived through it.

Finding the right person to work with is not simple, and I failed miserably. However, getting let go by Jonathan apparently brings luck and a lot of value. So those of you who have been fired — enjoy it. It's going to bring you a lot of luck. And I have many more names. I didn't want to bring them all up here, but it really does bring good luck.

So — leadership. By the way, because I'm talking about people, and many of you probably have questions — if you have any question at this point, just raise your hand and we'll make it really personal.

So each CEO is unique, and obviously, me being a CEO, I must be unique. CEOs have a DNA, and the DNA of a company is usually dictated by the CEO. I now witness a really interesting thing — I sold ZoomInfo, there's a new CEO, and I happen to have a few people I keep in touch with at the company. I can witness the change in the DNA of the company, for better and for worse — it's just different. The way I used to run the company and the way Henry runs the company is different. People who liked my style probably like what he's doing less, and people who worked well with him really enjoy what he's doing and didn't particularly like what I did. But it's just shifting to match the CEO's DNA. And that mismatch of style and personality is why good people with a good track record might fail. I brought enough examples of that before.

So I look at hiring as a very complex puzzle — putting together pieces that don't quite match. The example and the statistic I always bring is this: if there is anyone we spend a good amount of time evaluating before we bring them into our lives, it's our spouse, right? We date them. If they're not religious, you live with them for a year, two years, three years, you get married. And then 50% get divorced. And of the other 50%, half of them stay together because it's just too hard to get divorced. Why? Because it's difficult. Companies change, people change — it's very difficult to get right.

So I think I've convinced you that people is a complex equation and a complex riddle.

So what is the personality of a company? Let's start with myself, because it's the easiest thing to do — but I will later recommend that you all do this exercise too.

The first thing is: what is your philosophy about the company you built? I talked about it in one of the previous lectures — I played the infinite game. What is the infinite game? It's called life. We are all convinced that life is infinite. Each and every one of you in this room believes strongly that you're going to live forever — despite all the evidence to the contrary. As I keep telling my kids, there are two kinds of people in this world. There's you — and then there are people who are born old. They don't walk around like you do. They're born old, and you think you'll never get there. But unfortunately, yes, we do.

So when I build a company, I think about it as something I'm going to do for the rest of my life. And therefore, it better be great, and it better evolve over time.

What is a finite game? A finite game is very clearly defined. There are rules — it's like football, like basketball, like hockey. Two groups, rules, a set amount of time: 90 minutes, 60 minutes, whatever it is. And there are winners and losers, period. In the venture capital world, the equivalent is: you must have an exit. There is an end game — it's not infinite. You better sell or take the company public within seven years. That's it. So it's a very different DNA for a company — do you work toward a very clear target, or do you work like you're building it forever?

You better sell or take the company public within seven years. That's it. So it's a very different DNA for the company. Do you work towards a very clear target, or do you work like, okay, we're going to build it forever?

If you are going to build it forever, then you need to tell people where they're going. Because otherwise we're just walking the desert. For every company that I was involved in, we always put some — I call it the flag on the hill, or the flag on the mountain — guys, that's what we want to be when we grow up. And we never get there, of course, because I keep raising the flag. But it's the direction we all go. And clearly you've heard me say: Startup Academy aims to teach entrepreneurs how to build successful companies — profitable, fast growing, and with modest investment. There is a reason I repeat it every single time. It doesn't tell you the how, but it tells you where you want to be. And that's very important.

Because if you want to play an infinite game and you want to keep doing it for years, you need to have a clear target that everybody buys into. Okay, so what's beyond that — below that — what is it we seek and appreciate? Measurable results. The opposite of measurable results is: "Oh, I worked so hard, Jonathan. The whole weekend I was working, I can't even sleep, honestly." Why do you do that? I don't want you to work hard. I want you to bring results. If you can do it while you sleep, that's great. Working hard is an excuse. It means you are not thinking about what you do. People ask me, you know, you went to companies all at once — what did you do? I said I work 50 hours a week. That's what I work. Why 50 hours a week, 10 hours a day?

Those of you who know me here — I never show up before 11. Why? I get up at 6:30, 7:00 in the morning. But the morning I spend with my family, and I come home at 9. So 11 to 9 is not even 10 hours — it is 10 hours. That's it. I never work over a weekend. Why? Because I don't think that hard work gets you anywhere. You just have to decide: how do you measure your work?

Second, transparency. I just told you about all my failures, right? I think it works really well when you don't keep any secrets. The only secrets we have in a company are usually compensation and decision making. How do you make decisions in a company? And it also ties into transparency.

What I've found in other situations is that people have this vague way of how decisions are being made. It comes from the top and goes down. And these smart people at the top decided that this is it, based on everything they've learned. They tell you: this is what we do. Nonsense. If you can't explain to people why you made a decision, it's probably the wrong decision. It's that simple. And if you can't explain it because there are reasons you don't want to share, that's probably really bad. Because those reasons make it seem like you're doing something either illegal or something you don't want people to know. So if you don't want people to know — don't do it. So transparency and decision making, in my mind, go hand in hand.

What I did in all my companies was hold a company meeting once a month. In that meeting, we usually started with the financials. Remember, the company has to be profitable. There are no secrets. So we showed people: here are the revenues, here are the expenses, and hopefully the difference between them is positive. And if it was negative, we spent a good amount of time talking about why it was negative. It got to the point where people were bored and said, "Why do we do that every month? I don't want to hear again about the financials and all of that stuff." So after a while I said, okay, we'll do it on a quarterly basis — and you'll see later on why we do it on a quarterly basis.

But I think that being overly transparent is better than being secretive. The other concept I have is — as I've said many times — people are complex. People are different, and therefore they think differently than you. They might not be smarter than you, but they think differently than you. And it's very important to hear other angles on anything, because it opens your mind. Just this moment — where's Uthi? She said, "You know, I've been here for 10 or 12 lectures and suddenly somebody says, why don't we connect the power to this outlet?" She said that power outlet was there all the time, and she always tried to run the line from here to there — and there's an outlet right there. Okay? When different people look at something, they always find something you didn't think about.

Recognition. We'll get to it later, but I think it's one of the most important elements in management. If there's anything people hate, it's being invisible, being ignored. "Hi guys, how you doing? Wow, great, right? You're working hard, right?" and then moving on. I've seen enough CEOs come in and say, "Guys, you know, we have to do this, we're going to crush it," and then walk away. People see through that in about two seconds. But if you go to somebody and say, "What are you working on? Can you show me?" — at first people are like, what? What do you want? I used to travel — every three weeks I was in Boston. And what I used to do is walk down the corridors. By that time we had about 100 people at the company, and I'd randomly walk into one of the cubicles, introduce myself — because I didn't recognize everyone — and ask, "What are you working on?" People were like, "Oh, the CEO is asking — oh my God." And I was genuinely interested in what they were working on. When they did a nice job, I said, "You did a nice job." When they didn't, I said, "You know, you can do better than that — if we did it this way. And by the way, why didn't you talk to Joe? Joe is working on something very similar. The two of you should work together."

After a while, people got used to it. And they were actually really upset if I didn't stop by and talk to them, because they wanted me to. And I thought it was good that they were upset when I didn't, because it meant they felt like what they were doing mattered every morning.

As we say here, we are here to have fun. So yes — what do I mean by "have fun"? Have fun is not: we organize parties and go on trips and all of that. That's okay, but "have fun" means you genuinely enjoy what you're doing. You get up in the morning and say, "I can do this today, and I can do that today. I'm going to check this and check that." They enjoy what they're doing at work — not around work, but at work.

And how do you accomplish that? The way I do it is really simple. Each and every one of you — remember, you're all different — so each and every one of you has skills that are just not in your job description. Some of us like to create spreadsheets and calculate things. Others like to draw. Other people like to talk on the phone — if they don't talk to people, they feel lonely and miserable. Other people, if you ask them to be on the phone, they collapse. We're all different. I remember hiring a saleswoman, and in the interview I asked her, "A sales job means being on the phone." And she said, "Obviously, that's what I do all day long."

Fine. Then she joins the company, and her sales numbers aren't great. And every time I look over, she's never on the phone. So I go to her and say, "How come you're never on the phone?" She says, "Oh, I prepare — I prepare my pitch, I look things up on the computer." And at the end I said, "You just don't like talking on the phone, right?" She said, "Yeah." I said, "So what are you doing in sales?"

So each and every one of us is different, with different skills and different things we enjoy. What I usually do is watch what people do — not what they tell me they do. Because they don't lie in what they do; they think you're not going to notice. They don't lie there. Then I think, okay, this person really likes to write — they're very good at it. So let's shift a lot of the writing work to them. He's not in marketing? I don't care. He likes to write, so let's have him write. And this person likes to be on the phone? He's in engineering? So what? Let's just ask him to talk to customers. And when you start mixing the work so that people do what they really enjoy doing — and you ignore the rigid frames of job descriptions — you get a lot more done, a lot more fun, and you break a lot of the politics. Because you're basically saying: I don't care about your job description. I care about results. And if we can get the results while people are happy, I'm fine with it.

Now, obviously you don't do stupid things. But the more you attend to what people love doing, the better the results you get.

And what's written here is: no politics. If anything ruins a company, it's politics. Politics usually start when you move from one person to two. That's when you start having politics. Some people have politics even with one — my wife can attest to that — but that's just how we are. Let's be honest. We're human beings, we have all kinds of issues. Move from two to three, politics is guaranteed. Move from two to twenty, you have politics. But if you really focus on telling people: the moment you start doing politics and talking about territory — that's a no. Why should they do that? Because the moment you allow it to happen, it grows and it mushrooms.

So when I hire people, I always look for the no-ego type. The way they talk — is it "me, me" all the time, or is it "we, we"? Do they talk about what they've personally accomplished, or do they talk about the project? They talk about what they were trying to do, the results of it — and the "me" and the "we" is secondary. It's the project they were trying to do that keeps them excited. When people tell me "it's not my job," I ask them why. Because "it's not my job" is usually the end of it.

So let me move to the second point. I usually try to hire top-notch people. Why? Because chances are they'll be more successful. But top-notch people typically expect top-notch salaries. I tell them upfront: "Listen, I'm going to pay average salaries for your role. That's what I can afford to pay, because we have to be profitable." And what happens next is very interesting. There are two kinds of people. Those who say, "If I don't get that salary, I'm not coming." And I say, "Well, there's your answer. Thank you so much." And they go to another company and probably get more money. Or they say, "I really wanted more — but this company seems exciting. I've talked to a few people here, everybody seems excited, the projects are interesting. Okay, fine, I'm in."

Bonus plans. So another pet peeve. Why do companies give bonuses? Honestly, I don't understand it. I just don't understand why companies give bonuses — it makes no sense. And I'll explain why it makes no sense. Usually the bonus plans contain two parameters: your performance and the company's performance. Let's start with your performance. So end of the year, you had a $20,000 bonus if you perform. Now you have a choice.

You can either give him the $20,000 because you don't want to fight or cause offense, or you're going to have a very serious conversation about why you are not going to give the bonus. So instead of a bonus plan, I do profit sharing. What is profit sharing? It's a really simple idea — if there is a flag on the hill. Remember, I try to keep concepts really simple — the flag on the hill. Number one in a successful company is profits. Number two is it's your team who built the company, not you.

So if the team managed to create a successful company making money, then they should participate in it. So we took 20% of the profits and distributed it among all the people in the company as essentially a salary raise. When the company was doing well in the last four or five years of ZoomInfo, it was about a 10 to 11 to 12% increase across the board for everybody in the company every year. That sent two very strong messages.

Number one: we care about profitability. So I was able to walk up to anybody in the company and ask them, how do you contribute to profitability? And there are only two answers — either what you do increases the top line, or what you do decreases the expense line. If you don't fall into one of those two, then you have to ask yourself how you can do either. And unless you can explain it, maybe you should start looking in the mirror and figure out how you fit in. That was a very strong message that I didn't have to go and articulate — it was clear to everybody: you have to contribute to profitability.

Number two: people felt that they were participating, because the bonus was tied to something they could understand. Third, we did it on a quarterly basis. I won't bore you with all the details of how we did it, but every quarter we distributed profit sharing. Remember I said we moved the company meetings to once a quarter — so now there was a real reason for a quarterly meeting. And they watched the financials like hawks. Like hawks.

They wanted to see the top line, and sometimes they argued with me about the expenses. Everybody became a financier. So what are the laws about team size? Luckily, many people have researched this and there are rules. Parkinson's Law: work will expand to fill the time allotted for its completion. Which means if you have a day and you have a job that needs to get done, it will take you a day. Or as my mother used to say — that's the hard-boiled egg for Shabbat. Let me explain. My mother started cooking for Shabbat on Wednesday. By Thursday she had the entire meal ready for Shabbat, except for the hard-boiled egg. Why? I don't know. So it doesn't matter how difficult or short the job is — if you have a day to do it, it will take you a day. If you don't have time, it'll take you five minutes. So then, out of curiosity, he asked himself, let's look at the distribution of results. He took a subject and realized that there were about 1,000 articles on this subject. And these thousand articles were written by 100 different writers altogether. Then he asked himself, who are the people who wrote many articles? To his utter surprise, he discovered that if there were 1,000 articles and 100 writers, then the square root of the number of writers — which is 10 — wrote half of the articles. So 10 people did 50% of the work. The other 90 did the other 50% of the work. Square root. Remember, that means the efficiency of this is horrible.

If you fire the other 90, you still get 50% of the work done at 10% of the cost. That's basically the 80/20 rule, which was defined by Mr. Pareto. Pareto is the name of a person. So it happens in every single job. The 80/20 rule, or Price's Law — which means if you start building a company and you don't want to build a large organization beneath you, and you don't want to measure your success by the number of people working for you, but you really want to get the job done — focus on getting the job done. And you can do it with a very small number of highly talented people. And I have laws to prove that I'm right. They have nice names — Parkinson's Law and Price's Law — but they're really important.

So small teams are far more productive and efficient. More people does not mean faster results. So let me give you another insight. You have an engineer, and he's doing a really good job, but there's more work than one engineer can do. You bring another engineer, and the two of them sit in the same cubicle and start working. You know the story. The two of them become really good friends and work like a team. It's enough that one of them raises a finger and the other one knows exactly what he wants to do. It's phenomenal. One plus one equals two and a half — it works really well. So the boss says, it seems like you guys are really doing a good job. Why don't we hire more people? It seems like you really know what you're doing.

So they bring in a third person. Three people — wait a minute. Three people is a team. Who is going to manage these three people? So let's make one of them a team lead. Right there you have friction: each one of them wanted to be the team lead, and the two that didn't get it are now angry. But never mind, let's just move past it. The team lead now thinks: I'm a team lead, so what do I need to do? Clearly, we need to have team meetings. Remember before, they just kind of whispered, "What do I do here?" Done. But now we have team meetings. And wait a minute — there are other team leads in the organization, so we need to have a meeting of the team leaders. Now the team leaders want to get promoted, and so on and so forth. Before you know it, the whole organization starts dealing with itself instead of with productivity. And it happens in every single organization. It's just a side effect of growing your team, and it's very difficult not to fall into that trap. Very, very difficult.

You avoid it as much as you can. So if you are successful, eventually you have a company — so you do what I did: I sold it and moved on. No, I'm joking. What do you do? It's not easy. That was one of the biggest issues I dealt with all the time: how do you grow the organization without growing the bureaucracy? It's not simple, but it can be done. If you're focused, it can be done, but you really have to resist. People say, "I'm managing too many people, I don't have time for this, I don't have time for that." And you basically tell them: just stop managing. Delegate. Hire smart people. Let them work.

As I said, you have to hire the right people, and it's very difficult to figure out who the right people are. I've been talking about it for an hour and a half — I started by saying people are the biggest problem of a company. I don't have miracle solutions, but at least I can present the problems. These are real problems. They happen in every organization. My solution is the third point: smart people can be multidisciplinary.

The fact that somebody is an engineer doesn't mean that's the only thing they know how to do in life. They have other talents as well. Some of them really like to design what's on the screen. Some of them really like to talk to people, and they can do it well. Some of them like to do QA — I know some people like that — they enjoy finding bugs in other people's work. People are multidisciplinary. They like doing things that are not just the piece of code they need to write or the article they need to write. And if you keep talking to them and find out what else they like to do, you can start spreading the work among them. Does it solve all the problems? No. But one of the biggest missions I had in my companies was to keep the team small. I know it sounds foolish, but that's the way it is.

One of my biggest joys — you know, when people were raising money like crazy and I met somebody and I said, "So how is it going?" — "Unbelievable, we grew like crazy, we're growing so fast." I said, "What do you mean?" He said, "We used to be 50 people last month and now we're 100 people." And I said, okay, that's about one month before you shut down — because you brought 50 new people into the company, you don't know their names, they don't know each other. It's going to be a disaster. But they felt successful because they doubled the organization in one month. It's a huge success in their eyes.

I look at it as a huge disaster. But that's the way people look at growth: the more people I have, the more successful I am. And they don't remember this equation I put up earlier. Available time is money in the bank divided by your expenses. They didn't understand that if you hire another 50 people, your money will not last long — which means you have to go raise money again.

Okay, let's move on. Then there is the hidden structure, which also relates to the point above. Every company has an org chart — that's the official structure of the company. There's the CEO, there are the VPs, the director level, the manager level. It always looks like a tree. But in reality, that's not the way companies work. The way they actually work is through real influences.

There's a very interesting study done by MIT. What they did is they put an RFID tag on people's clothing, so that when they got close together, they started to exchange signals — basically recording who was talking to whom. So they figured out where people spend their time and who they're talking to outside of the org chart. What they discovered was that the people others liked to come and talk to were very different from the official org chart.

For example — in our company, remember the famous Donna? Everybody in the company talked to her at least once a week. Why? Because she was funny, she knew all the gossip, and she had a very sharp tongue. So you usually came out with some wisdom about yourself that you didn't like, but it was funny. Okay, so everybody talked to her.

We also had somebody in engineering — she was very good, she's still there — and she came in with one condition: "I don't want to be a manager. I don't want the responsibility." And she was the hub of the engineers, because she's very smart. People would come to her for real advice, and she would sit with them and help them and build things. She was a big hub. And she said, "I don't want to be a manager. Don't make me a manager. Why? What a waste of time. Running around in meetings, all of that, doing planning — I don't want it. I just do my job." And she's really great.

So there's always this hidden org chart. A good manager tries to figure it out and leverage it, because somehow it represents the actual skill set much better than anything in your official org chart. People know who can help them, people know who can do what. And if you just follow these hidden actual influences, you can improve the efficiency of your organization — and everybody is happy. That's the beautiful thing about it. Because people are already going to that person anyway. All you have to do is give that person responsibility for the things that people come and talk to them about, which leads to this: leverage the people you have before you hire more.

Or, my conclusion — if it wasn't clear until now — hire as few people as possible. Remember, you need to be profitable. You need time to build your company. Hire as few people as possible. Every person adds overhead. As I said before, you have two people, you add another person — now he's a team lead, and so on. You have 20 people, you need an HR function, you need annual reviews, and so on. People create work around them.

As I said before: ignore titles, shift tasks around, give people tasks they enjoy doing. Keep a very flat, fluid, dynamic organization. It sounds like a disaster — it worked for me. I'm again talking from my own perspective. Other managers will behave differently, but it has to work with your personality.

What happens if you have somebody that doesn't fit? Act swiftly — you have to let them go, and it's better to do it sooner rather than later.

How do you get the know-how? In many cases you bring in people who don't have the specific know-how. But does that mean you need to hire someone with the know-how? My approach is: there is know-how out there, but that doesn't mean you need to hire that person. You can get the know-how without hiring them full-time. How? You bring them in on an hourly basis — even if they charge you $500 an hour. In many cases, it's much cheaper than hiring a full-time person. All you need to do is find the people who really have the know-how and that you want to work with. For example, SEO. Okay, hiring. Before I start going into hiring, I have to admit — as I've already said it about 100 times in this meeting — I don't know how to hire. I just don't. He said a month later, "I think that the person who shows up at work is not the person I hired. It must be somebody else, because nothing of what I saw in the interview is in this person who shows up." And it happened to me many times. You just get really excited in the interview process. You really like what you hear, you think this is great, and then the person shows up and after a few weeks you say, "This is not the person I interviewed. What happened?"

Okay, I don't have a solution. Don't misunderstand me. I'm just stating that what I'm talking about is probably what happens everywhere. When people come to HR, they say, "We have a process that really gets the right people in the door."

No, but you have a solution. Because you mentioned before that if you have the option to work with someone on an hourly basis, maybe as a freelancer or something like that, and to test it over three months—

You're right, but that's only if that person is available. A lot of companies try to pull people out of competitors, try to pull people out of anywhere. It's just hard. I mean, I don't have solutions. All I'm trying to say is: why do I want to keep a small team? Because a smaller team means you need to do less hiring, so you make fewer mistakes. That's all. It's really as simple as that.

Okay. What I'm looking for — at least I define for myself what I'm looking for. So I'm looking for three things. And again, can I guarantee that I get what I'm defining here? No.

But I'm looking for three elements. Number one: very smart. A lot of very smart people get bored very quickly. So you give them a problem, they think about it, and then they move on. What do you mean, move on? They solved it in their head, so it's not interesting anymore. Nothing happened in your company — they solved it. They're already on to the next thing. I hired enough PhDs to fill a university. I fired more of them. It's like they come in, they're really smart, they look at the problem, they dig into it, and then they move on. And you say, "What happened?" And they say, "I solved the problem." And I say, "Where are the results?" And they say, "Oh, for that, bring an engineer — it's not interesting anymore."

So I want people who are focused on results. I don't care whether you solved it or not — show me that it works. And again, I'm looking for people who do it inherently for themselves, not for me. They don't think they solved it until they see it working with their own eyes. So it's the quality of the person, not the way I manage. The quality of the person is: very smart and results-oriented. They only care about results, and they have no ego. No ego means they do the work because they enjoy doing it. That's what gives them the satisfaction — not the promotion, not the ego, not "I, I, I." They just want to do the thing — that's what they want to do in life. Then you get great results. Very hard to find them.

If I haven't made it clear until now — I think I'm repeating myself. Right. It's the most complex problem you're trying to solve, and it's multi-dimensional. Why? Because you want somebody with the skills, the brains, the experience, the personality, the attitude, salary expectations, commitment, yada, yada. By the time you're done with the list, you're left with no candidates.

Yes. When were you happy with the people you hired? Very simple. I hired and fired and hired and was excited. That's it. Number three — always number three. So I wish I could get to number three before I go and do number one, number two. No, I'm serious. It's just trial and error — and it's great, and you love the person and you're doing great things together. Hard to predict.

I'm actually talking to the person who was the co-founder of ZoomInfo in the year 2000. He was the CTO, engineer — whatever you want to call him. We were two people building the company. And so he's done great since then, and called me about a year ago saying maybe we can do something together. Then decided — he's in Boston, I'm here — he went in a different direction. He called me the other day and said, "Let's talk," because we worked really well together and we did great things.

So who would you hire? I gave you two options. An experienced person who did this specific job you need two or three times already — so you interview the guy and he says, "Yeah, Company X, I did that. And Company Y, I did exactly the same thing. I know exactly what you want and I can do it for you." Or the up-and-comer. So he says, "I wanted to do what you need, but I had a boss sitting there — so instead of building from beneath, I just left. And I would love to get that job. I want to move to the next level. I was a manager, I want to be a director."

Who would you hire? The experienced person or the up-and-comer?

The hungry one. The hungry one.

What about their experience? Usually if you did the same job three times, you'd be bored. Smart and bored. Peter Principle. In an organization, every employee tends to rise to their level of incompetence. What does that mean? You start at the entry level, you're doing a really great job, so you get promoted. You're doing a great job, you get promoted. You're doing a great job, you get promoted. You're doing a lousy job — you don't get fired, you just get stuck there. That's it.

So there is a good chance that the people in the higher echelons are the failures. Totally counterintuitive, but that's exactly what happens. So when I look at a resume and I see a person doing three or four jobs at basically the same level, that's the answer — that's their level of incompetence. So why would I want to hire them?

You answered exactly right. So remember that. That's the Peter Principle. I told you about Parkinson, I told you about Price, I told you about Peter. So at least I have big guys to stand under.

Okay, another hiring dilemma. A person with 20 years of experience who wants a high salary, or a person with much less experience at a much lower salary. Well, the problem with the higher-paid person many times is that he's already at a stage in his career where he just doesn't want to do the work. So for 80,000 shekels a month, he wants to manage — he doesn't want to work anymore. So he might present himself as, "Yes, I'm a great engineer," but in reality he wants to be a manager. So he keeps hiring more people. Chances are, if you see a person like that — unless you really know that person very well and have worked with him — you're going to get into this situation. And as I said before, you can get outside advice from people.

Okay, let's move on. So how? Well, salaries match a person's performance. Does a higher salary make a person work harder? All of you say no. So why do we pay them a higher salary? So you don't lose them. What I found is that salary is not a motivator. People feel that if you give a bonus, give more salary, people will work harder. In reality, it never works — but the opposite does happen. So if you take a person who can make, let's say, 40,000 shekels a month and you convince them to come and work for 25,000 shekels a month at your company, there's a good chance that will become a demotivator because they have to scale down their expenses at home. It causes a lot of friction. It's difficult. So taking a person and not giving them what they need is a huge demotivator.

Taking a person who made 25,000 and giving them 40 is not a motivation, because two weeks later they assume that's the salary they deserve to get. And now they want 45. So you have to be very careful about this.

So I have seen people try to do the 100%, but they can't afford the salary and they start inventing all kinds of crazy ideas — "if you hit these KPIs, we'll give you this, we'll give you that." It's just putting landmines along your way.

Salary comparison — again. One of the things I've learned the hard way is that there are two kinds of comparisons. There is the salary I can get somewhere in the market, and there is the salary I get here. So let's take engineers as an example — but it applies everywhere.

So if an engineer says, "I'm a full-stack engineer, I have five years of experience, I've worked at all of these companies, I should make 35,000" — okay. He comes to the company, he meets with me — being a cheap guy, I say, "I can't afford 35." I convinced the guy to take 30. But he says, "I can make 35, I can make even 40." And I tell the person, "You're right, but I pay average salaries. So if you want to work with Libby and Ayala, you have to be okay with 30." And I convinced him. And he won't look outside anymore because he made a decision — he decided to stay.

Then one day he discovers that the guy sitting in the cubicle next to him is making 45,000. And in his mind, this guy is not as good an engineer as he is. That person will leave the company the following day. Happened to me. Why? Because now it's not about salary — it's an insult. It became personal. What he can make outside is a vague concept. But if inside the company he finds injustice — in his mind, blatant injustice — he sees that as an insult, and he will leave. Sorry for using "he" all the time — the women will leave too.

Where is the problem? The problem starts with something even more insidious. You have engineers, you pay them 30,000 shekels, and you're dying for this engineer who knows Elasticsearch. And it's hard to find Elasticsearch people. So you finally find somebody and he wants 50,000 shekels, and you're desperate, so you agree.

You have engineers, you pay them $30,000, and you're dying to find this engineer who knows Elasticsearch. And it's hard to find these Elasticsearch people. So you finally find somebody and he wants $50,000, and you're desperate, so you agree.

So you pay that person $50,000 — 50,000 shekels a month. And it turns out, like in most of my descriptions, that he's an okay engineer. He maybe knows Elasticsearch, but he's an okay engineer, nothing too sophisticated. But now you're stuck with all your people making 30,000 and one of them making 50,000, and he's okay, he's not shining. You have two choices. You fire him — and you shouldn't have hired him to begin with. He didn't do anything wrong. He's an engineer at the same level as your other engineers. So in the dismissal, the only thing you can say is: I made a mistake. Well, that's not a reason to fire me. You made a mistake, okay? I'm serious. That's the problem. You don't have a problem firing people who don't perform. That's easy. You don't have a problem firing people who don't show up for work.

That's easy. You have a problem firing people who are okay. They're just not as good as you want them to be. You have no really objective reason to fire the person. So that's one of the things I was always tremendously worried about when people came to me wanting way above the average salary for that position in my company. I would say, listen, you're not going to cost me 50,000 instead of 30,000. You're going to cost me 200,000. He says, why? I said, because I have 10 other people whose salaries I now need to raise to 50. There's no way I can do that. I'm sorry, I can't hire you. Because the day they discover that person made much more money than them is the day they start leaving. People are complex.

Now it's a personal insult. So that's why salaries and compensation are not transparent. That's what I just described. Same goes for bonus plans, as I described before. What's the problem with bonus plans? Most bonus plans — the personal ones, not the company ones — are tied to KPIs. If you accomplish this and this... remember, it's a year, it's an annual plan. So you build KPIs for the whole year. But remember, we are a startup. We don't have experience. This is not a railroad or a bank where you have 30 years of experience and know what to expect. You build these KPIs based on what you think right now you want to accomplish. But two months into it you're wiser and you want to change the plan. Happens all the time. All the time.

Now you can just go and say, we changed the plan. So I want you to focus on this other thing now, and you say, sure — what do we want to accomplish? You sit down, make a decision, move on, and you're as happy as can be. But if your salary now depends on it, you say, wait a minute, I was working towards that KPI and I'm about two weeks before we launch X, which I'm going to make money on. You can't really change it. You just can't. My salary depends on it. So suddenly you've taken the flexibility of the company to move with the flow and turned it into something rigid. You can't change because people's salaries depend on it. Every conversation becomes emotional and loaded. That's the insidious problem of bonus plans.

That's why I don't allow bonus plans in my companies. There are no personal bonuses — there is profit sharing. We're all tied to only one thing: making money. And when we make money, we share it. But we cannot build bonus plans. So when people come in and say, okay, I can't pay you the 50,000 you want, but if you release that product by that date I'll give you 10,000 shekels — and if you do this I'll give you that — you start building these very complex plans to avoid the salary issue, and you're just building landmine after landmine. It's going to blow up in your face.

You know, you mentioned profit sharing and you stated it as a bonus. Not as a bonus, but as a raise in salary. But a raise in salary is something constant — you don't reduce the salary. So why not have a yearly — I can call it a bonus — but a profit share that is just a one-time profit share, then next year based on next year's profit? Again, we do it like that. Except that profit sharing, as the name implies, is not a bonus — it's profit sharing. No profit, no sharing. The amount shared is linear with the profit. If you want, I can show you how I build it. It's not overly complex, but the way it is communicated matters. Because remember — how do you explain profit sharing? Let's say we made a million dollars. What does that mean to my pocket? You can't really talk about a million dollar profit split among 50 people. It just doesn't land.

So what we did is we said: for every half a million — or a million, depending on the stage of the company — for every half a million dollars during the year, each one of you will get 1% of your salary as a bonus. Now we can count how much money we put in the bank, and we share that. And remember, we had weekly, monthly, and quarterly meetings, so we showed them the numbers.

But you said "raise" again. That's what confuses me.

No, it's not a raise. You will get 1% of your salary as a bonus. And you know exactly what the bonus is — it's 1% of my salary. It was based on your cumulative salary up to that point in time. So at the end of Q1, it was only three months' salary times 1%, which ended up being $300 or $500.

People said, that's not profit sharing, that's a joke. The following quarter, we already had a million and a half dollars in the bank. So it's 3%, but it's 3% on salary for the first half of the year — six months. So suddenly instead of $500, it was $2,000. And people started to say, wow, that's really interesting. And in the last quarter, which included the full year's salary and a lot more profit, they got a huge bonus. And people were totally psyched. So it worked really well. It's just the way the equations worked. But it wasn't guaranteed — it depended on how much money we put in the bank. And they could see it.

So people ask me, how do you keep morale in a company? And the answer is really simple. When the company does well, morale is high. When the company does badly, morale falls. That's about as simple as it gets. You can try to talk about it and do all kinds of things, but people see through it. If your company is not doing well, morale is low. When the company is doing well, everybody is excited. So try to do well.

People strive for attention. I talked about it. My famous example is when you have a kid — 2 years old, 3 years old — the words they say all the time are: look, Mom; look, Dad; look at what I'm doing. They want attention, total attention. Which is why we go crazy when we have little kids — they want full-time attention. When we grow up, we still want full-time attention, but it's impolite. We behave like we don't want it. But we do. Never forget that. People want attention. I even know a prime minister who refuses to leave because he wants attention all the time. And he's a grown-up. So people want attention.

So companies do Employee of the Month. Let me explain to you how Employee of the Month works. You have 50 people in the company and you have three, four, five stars — that's usually the number. So the first month it's really simple. You take the one who is truly phenomenal, who does everything. She's phenomenal. You give her Employee of the Month, everybody claps and cheers, and so on.

The second month it's the second star, and it's very simple to do, and you're very happy. The fifth month it's number five on your list, and that's still good. The sixth month you want to give it again to the first employee, because she really is a star. But you can't give Employee of the Month to the same person month after month, because the whole idea is to share it. But these are the only five people you really want to give it to. So what do you do? You scratch around and find employee number six, and you find a reason to say you're doing a great job. And then employee number seven. And when you get to employee number ten, you quietly discard the whole plan because it becomes ridiculous. Happens in every single company. Don't even start.

So forget Employee of the Month as a morale booster — it causes the opposite effect. Public recognition: what could be better than saying, guys, we just released our product. This was a great accomplishment. Jeroen, you did a wonderful job. You ran the whole thing wonderfully. Everybody claps. And then after the meeting, she comes to me and says, you know, I was so involved — you didn't even mention my name. I'm really insulted. How could you forget? I ran all the meetings. I did all the work. So I learned the hard way that when you mention people and congratulate them in public, they remember it for about an hour. The person you forgot remembers it for life. An hour or a lifetime — very dangerous.

So in 2018, I sold the company and we had a nice ceremony. I wanted to give a speech and thank the people who worked with me. So I decided I'm going to avoid this pitfall. I'm going to be smart. So I went to Donna — you remember her — and I said, Donna, please do me a favor. Give me the list of all the people who were at the company for at least 10 years, or whatever the number was, and make sure not to make a mistake. This is going to be dangerous. So she figured it out. She went through all the employment agreements and put together the list. I got a list of about 15 or 20 people.

And I said I'd really like to thank all the people, my co-founders, who were with me for at least 10 years. And I read their names and so forth. We finished, went to the buffet, and Donna comes to me and says, John is furious. He's crying. And I'm like, why? What happened? She said, you forgot to mention his name. I said, Donna, your job was to create the list. She said, on the list he's less than 10 years. But remember that ZoomInfo came out of CartScan — he used to work at CartScan 20 years ago. And then when you sold CartScan in 2006, you moved him to ZoomInfo, so he's clearly the most tenured person you have in the company. And I said, how did you miss that? She said, I looked at his employment agreement and it says the year 2006, or whatever it was. And I talked to him afterwards. He was so insulted, you can't believe it. So public recognition is really dangerous. Be careful.

So what do you do? I came up with a different solution, which I call a Night on the Town. What do you do? You go to Eyal and you say, Eyal, you did a wonderful job on everything you've been doing. I really appreciate it. Do me a favor — take your wife or significant other to the best restaurant in the next two weeks and bring me the invoice, up to $250. We'll pay. Just have a night on the town. Thanks, I really appreciate it.
Led "Night on Town." So what do you do when it's "Night on Town"? You go to Eyal and you say, "Eyal, you did a wonderful job on all the stuff you're doing. Really, I really appreciate it. Do me a favor — take your wife or significant other and take her to the best restaurant in the next two weeks and bring me the invoice, up to $250. We pay. Just have a night on the town. Thanks, I really appreciate it."

But do me a favor, keep it between you and your wife. Now, what happens? If I gave it to him as a bonus, he would start laughing at me — "What do you mean, a bonus of $250? That doesn't make any sense. It's too small for my contributions." So by doing that and keeping it quiet, other people don't get insulted because it's kind of between him and me. Second, I asked him to bring his wife or his significant other and to tell her, "Listen, remember I came home late so many times because I was working hard — the company recognized it." Third, chances are they are not going to spend $250 at a restaurant they usually don't go to. So it's kind of an event for them. He goes, takes his wife, they really have a good time.

He brings the invoice, I pay him. He feels special, and I can do it every quarter. He feels recognized, and it's quiet. So I used to do it a lot, because it's small money, big impact, avoids the pitfalls — hopefully it always did, but I tried at least. That's what I tried to do: recognize people, give them something that the people they care about — their wife, their husband, their kids sometimes — recognize that the company recognized it. In my experience, it didn't have the other side effects I described.

As I said, leadership has the highest impact. The other thing is, not always do things go well. What do you do when things don't go well? At least in my experience, hiding it doesn't work. People know. And the more you try to avoid talking about it, the bigger the issue becomes. The more you try to circumvent it, people will get more and more nervous. If you talk about it, it at least removes the secrecy around it. So if you have a hard time, the company is not meeting its targets — make it a public subject. Say, "Guys, we didn't meet our target. We're not making money this month. I need help. Can you help me think about how we make money again?" Sometimes they come up with a great idea. Many times they don't. But they feel that you share with them and that they can participate in the discussion. It reduces the tension.

If you need to lay off people, do it. You can't avoid laying off people. And laying off is not firing. In America, there is a very clear distinction. Firing is personal. A layoff is a group action — there's some sort of force majeure. Something happened in the environment: you close down a location, so everybody in that location has to go. So it's relatively straightforward to do.

I did it once in my life — remember the Palm Pilot story and so forth. That happened because the dot-com hype crashed and Palm Pilot started losing money like crazy, and we were tied to Palm Pilot's performance for various reasons. So when I saw that Palm Pilot was going down the drain, I said, "We need to take action now before it's too late." We decided to lay off a third of our people. We had about 50 people, so we decided to lay off 16 or 17.

Here's what we decided to do: each person on the management team — there were five executives — would independently create a ranked list. Number one was the person we most wanted to let go but were very anxious about — mainly lawsuits and so forth. At the bottom, number 15 or 16, was the person we really didn't want to let go but had to for cost reasons. Each one of you creates a list, and then we compare them. Surprisingly — or not surprisingly — the lists had a really strong overlap. We had all ranked people in terms of their contribution to the company in roughly the same order.

Then, I believe it was on a Friday morning, we called these people one after the other and basically said, "We're sorry, we have to do a layoff. Please go home, come back over the weekend, and pick up your things — but we need you to leave now." And after we finished those 16 or 17 calls, we called the rest of the company together and said, "Everybody sitting in this room right now is here to stay." We explained why we did what we did, and why we cut a little more than we thought we strictly needed to — because we wanted to make sure that everyone staying knew they were safe, that we had plenty of revenue and money to continue operations.

And as we expected, about a week later it wasn't the subject anymore. The first day, obviously, people were rattled. By Monday, people were still rattled — but then it disappeared. It just disappeared, because they understood: this was a one-time, very deep cut, and that's it. It was the only time, luckily for me, that I had to do a layoff. But if you have to do it — do it quickly, do it big, and get it done with.

Now, let's do the summary. People are complex. If I haven't convinced you of that by now, then you are very linear in your thinking. People are complex, people are unique. And honestly, if you can convince me that you know how people will behave, you're a genius — I'm not. I told you about my personal experiences. We discussed co-founders and how much I think they are a huge benefit. Team size — keep it small. Hiring — complex. Compensation — difficult. Life is hard, morale is low.

So that was it.

הוא מביא את החשבונית, אני משלם לו. הוא מרגיש מיוחד, ואני יכול לעשות את זה כל רבעון. הוא מרגיש מוכר, וזה בשקט. אז הרבה פעמים הייתי עושה את זה, כי זה כסף קטן, השפעה גדולה, מונע את המלכודות — בתקווה תמיד עשה, אבל לפחות ניסיתי. זה מה שניסיתי לעשות: להכיר באנשים, לתת להם משהו שהאנשים שאכפת להם מהם — אשתם, בעלם, ילדיהם לפעמים — מכירים בכך שהחברה הכירה בזה. מניסיוני, לא היו לזה תופעות הלוואי האחרות שתיארתי.

כפי שאמרתי, ל-leadership יש את ההשפעה הגבוהה ביותר. הדבר האחר הוא שלא תמיד הדברים הולכים טוב. מה עושים כשדברים לא הולכים טוב? לפחות מניסיוני, הסתרה לא עובדת. אנשים יודעים. וככל שאתם מנסים יותר להימנע מלדבר על זה, הבעיה גדלה יותר. ככל שאתם מנסים יותר לעקוף אותה, אנשים יהיו יותר ויותר עצבניים. אם אתם מדברים על זה, זה לפחות מסיר את החשאיות סביב זה. אז אם יש לכם קשיים, החברה לא עומדת ביעדים שלה — הפכו את זה לנושא ציבורי. אמרו, "חבר'ה, לא עמדנו ביעד שלנו. אנחנו לא מרוויחים כסף החודש הזה. אני צריך עזרה. האם אתם יכולים לעזור לי לחשוב על איך אנחנו שוב מרוויחים כסף?" לפעמים הם מגיעים עם רעיון נהדר. פעמים רבות הם לא. אבל הם מרגישים שאתם חולקים איתם ושהם יכולים להשתתף בדיון. זה מפחית את המתח.

אם אתם צריכים לפטר אנשים, עשו את זה. אתם לא יכולים להימנע מלפטר אנשים. ופיטורי צוות הם לא פיטורים. באמריקה, יש הבחנה ברורה מאוד. פיטורים הם אישיים. פיטורי צוות הם פעולה קבוצתית — יש מעין כוח עליון. משהו קרה בסביבה: אתם סוגרים מיקום, אז כולם באותו מיקום צריכים ללכת. אז זה יחסית פשוט לעשות.

עשיתי את זה פעם אחת בחיי — זכרו את סיפור Palm Pilot וכן הלאה. זה קרה כי הייפ הדוט-קום קרס ו-Palm Pilot התחיל להפסיד כסף כמו משוגע, ואנחנו היינו קשורים לביצועי Palm Pilot מסיבות שונות. אז כשראיתי ש-Palm Pilot שוקע, אמרתי, "אנחנו צריכים לפעול עכשיו לפני שיהיה מאוחר מדי." החלטנו לפטר שליש מהאנשים שלנו. היו לנו כ-50 אנשים, אז החלטנו לפטר 16 או 17.

הנה מה שהחלטנו לעשות: כל אדם בצוות הניהולי — היו חמישה מנהלים — יכין בצורה עצמאית רשימה מדורגת. מספר אחד היה האדם שהכי רצינו לשחרר אבל היינו מאוד חרדים לגביו — בעיקר תביעות משפטיות וכן הלאה. בתחתית, מספר 15 או 16, היה האדם שממש לא רצינו לשחרר אבל היינו חייבים מטעמי עלויות. כל אחד מכם יוצר רשימה, ואז אנחנו משווים אותן. במפתיע — או לא במפתיע — היה לרשימות חפיפה חזקה ממש. כולנו דירגנו אנשים מבחינת תרומתם לחברה בסדר דומה מאוד.

ואז, אני מאמין שזה היה ביום שישי בבוקר, קראנו לאנשים האלה אחד אחרי השני ובעצם אמרנו, "אנחנו מצטערים, אנחנו צריכים לעשות פיטורי צוות. בבקשה לכו הביתה, חיזרו בסוף השבוע, ואספו את החפצים שלכם — אבל אנחנו צריכים שתעזבו עכשיו." ואחרי שגמרנו את אותם 16 או 17 שיחות, קראנו לשאר החברה יחד ואמרנו, "כל מי שיושב בחדר הזה עכשיו נשאר." הסברנו למה עשינו מה שעשינו, ולמה קצצנו קצת יותר ממה שחשבנו שצריך בהחלט — כי רצינו לוודא שכל מי שנשאר ידע שהוא בטוח, שיש לנו מספיק הכנסות וכסף להמשיך בפעילות.

ובאופן שציפינו, בערך שבוע לאחר מכן זה כבר לא היה הנושא. ביום הראשון, ברור, אנשים היו מטולטלים. ביום שני, אנשים עדיין היו מטולטלים — אבל אז זה נעלם. פשוט נעלם, כי הם הבינו: זה היה חתך חד-פעמי, עמוק מאוד, וזהו. זאת הייתה הפעם היחידה, למרבה מזלי, שהייתי צריך לעשות פיטורי צוות. אבל אם אתם צריכים לעשות את זה — עשו את זה מהר, עשו את זה גדול, וסיימו עם זה.

עכשיו, בואו נעשה סיכום. אנשים מורכבים. אם לא שכנעתי אתכם בזה עד עכשיו, אז אתם מאוד ליניאריים בחשיבה שלכם. אנשים מורכבים, אנשים ייחודיים. ובכנות, אם אתם יכולים לשכנע אותי שאתם יודעים איך אנשים יתנהגו, אתם גאונים — אני לא. סיפרתי לכם על הניסיונות האישיים שלי. דיברנו על co-founders וכמה אני חושב שהם יתרון עצום. גודל הצוות — שמרו אותו קטן. גיוס — מורכב. תגמול — קשה. החיים קשים, המורל נמוך.

אז זהו.

Lecture 13 of the SmartUp Foundations Course, delivered by Yonatan Stern, tackles what he considers the most complex dimension of building a successful business: people. Stern frames the entire discussion around a core tension — people are a company's most valuable asset and, simultaneously, the primary reason most businesses fail. This applies to both employees and customers, though the session focuses exclusively on the former.

Stern opens with a financial lens: in most companies, 70–80% of expenses are salaries and related costs, yet those same people represent 100% of a company's success or failure. Drawing on Galileo's insight that the universe is written in mathematics, he urges founders to translate every people-related decision into measurable financial terms — because money is the language of business, and it is the only reliable compass for direction.

A significant portion of the lecture addresses co-founders. Stern is candid about his own difficult experiences, having started his first company with five co-founders only to see the group fragment over power struggles and misaligned expectations. His conclusion is unconventional: rather than seeking a co-founder out of fear of loneliness or investor pressure, founders are better served by raising even a modest amount of capital and hiring their first key person as an employee. This preserves clarity of leadership and makes course-correction — including letting someone go — far simpler. When co-founders are chosen, complementary skills are essential; teams of engineers with identical backgrounds create redundancy, not strength.

On leadership, Stern emphasises authenticity, transparency, and restraint. He warns against public recognition, which can inadvertently breed resentment among peers, and instead advocates for quiet, personal gestures — such as his "Night on the Town" approach, where an employee is privately thanked and given a modest dining allowance to share with a partner. The impact is outsized precisely because it is personal and discreet.

When companies face hardship, Stern argues strongly for transparency. Hiding bad news amplifies anxiety; openly naming the problem invites collective problem-solving and reduces tension. When layoffs become necessary, his advice is equally direct: act quickly, cut deeply enough to restore genuine confidence in the remaining team, and communicate clearly. His own experience laying off 17 people during the dot-com crash illustrates how decisiveness, when paired with honest communication, allows a team to stabilise and move forward within days.

The lecture closes with a reminder that there are no simple formulas for managing people — only experience, humility, and the willingness to engage with complexity head-on.

ניהול אנשים הוא האתגר המורכב ביותר בבניית חברה, ואין לו פתרונות קסם. ההרצאה עוסקת בחוקים ארגוניים ידועים המסבירים מדוע ארגונים נוטים לנפח את עצמם, ובאסטרטגיות מעשיות להתמודד עם הכשלים הנפוצים בניהול צוותות.

חוק פרקינסון קובע שעבודה מתרחבת כדי למלא את הזמן הפנוי לביצועה. בארגונים, מנהלים מעדיפים לצמוח כלפי מטה — להוסיף עובדים — על פני קידום מעלה חסום. תופעה זו יוצרת בירוקרטיה הולכת וגדלה שעוסקת בעצמה במקום בפרודוקטיביות. חוק Price מוסיף ממד כמותי: השורש הריבועי ממספר העובדים מייצר מחצית מהתפוקה. כלומר, צוות קטן ומחונן עשוי לייצר תוצאות זהות לצוות גדול בעשירית העלות — זהו למעשה כלל ה-80/20 של פארטו. עיקרון פיטר משלים את התמונה: כל עובד נוטה להתקדם עד לרמת חוסר הכשירות שלו, כך שדווקא האנשים בדרגות הגבוהות הם לעיתים הכשלונות הגלויים.

בנוגע לגיוס, עדיף לבחור ב"רעב" — המועמד השאפתן שמחפש לעלות שלב — על פני המנוסה שחזר על אותה עבודה שלוש פעמים וסביר שהגיע לרמת חוסר הכשירות שלו. בנושא השכר, המסקנה המרכזית היא שמשכורת גבוהה אינה מניע לעבודה קשה יותר, אך אי-שוויון פנים-ארגוני — כשעובד מגלה שעמיתו מרוויח משמעותית יותר ממנו — הופך לפגיעה אישית ומוביל לפרישה מיידית.

בנוגע להכרה בעובדים, הכרה ציבורית מסוכנת: מי שלא הוזכר זוכר זאת לכל חייו. גישה יעילה יותר היא הכרה אישית ושקטה — למשל, הזמנה לארוחת ערב זוגית על חשבון החברה, בפרטיות. כך העובד מרגיש מוערך, בן זוגו שותף להכרה, ולא נוצרות תחושות קנאה או עלבון אצל אחרים.

לבסוף, כאשר מצב החברה קשה — שקיפות עדיפה על הסתרה. ואם נדרשים פיטורים המוניים, יש לבצעם מהר, בהיקף גדול ובפעם אחת, תוך הסבר לנשארים שהם יציבים ובטוחים. חיתוך חד-פעמי ועמוק מאפשר לארגון להתאושש מהר יותר מאשר אי-ודאות ממושכת. המסר המרכזי: שמרו על צוות קטן, גייסו בחכמה, הכירו בצנעה, ואל תמדדו הצלחה במספר העובדים.
